transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-03
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 34 minutes
Attendees: Liam Torres (Redwood AE), Sara Huang (Recruiter), Devon Park (Hiring Manager), Tereza Khan (Candidate)

Summary: First pass phone screen for ML Platform Engineer. Role focuses on serving/runtime, inference optimization, and infra automation. We cover resume walkthrough, system design around model serving at scale, kernel/quantization experience, oncall, and culture fit. Candidate has experience at HorizonBI working on inference pipelines and has run Triton/TF-Serving in production; interested in Redwood's runtime optimizations.

Topics: resume walkthrough; distributed inference; batching & KV cache; Triton vs custom runtime; quantization experience; Kubernetes & VPC/on-prem exposure; oncall and incident examples; next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam: Hey hi everyone, this is Liam with Redwood — thanks for joining, do you hear me okay?
[00:02] Tereza: Yep, loud and clear, thanks for having me.
[00:06] Sara: Hi Tereza, I'm Sara, I'm the recruiter — quick intro, we'll do 30-ish minutes and then next steps.
[00:12] Devon: Hi Tereza, Devon here, I'm the hiring manager, nice to meet you.
[00:15] Tereza: Hi all, excited to chat.
[00:20] Liam: Cool, quick framing: this is a phone screen to cover background and fit. We'll ask about production inference stacks, tradeoffs, and a couple of technical scenarios. Any questions before we start?
[00:28] Tereza: No, sounds great.
[00:30] Liam: Okay, can you walk us through the last two projects you worked on at HorizonBI, specifically anything related to serving large models or optimizing latencies?
[00:40] Tereza: Sure. Most recently I was on infra for our recommender inference — we run a two-stage pipeline, a candidate generation model on CPU and a re-ranker on GPU. We moved from TF-Serving to Triton for the re-ranker, because Triton handled multi-model ensembles better and gave us better batching controls.
[01:05] Tereza: We had to add prefix caching for user embeddings and implement a small KV cache in front of the re-ranker to avoid re-computing hot paths. The tricky bit was tail-latency — 95th percentile had spikes during peak traffic.
[01:20] Devon: How did you approach the tail-latency mitigation?
[01:24] Tereza: We implemented per-customer priority lanes and pre-warmed GPU instances during predicted spikes, and tuned batch sizes dynamically using a feedback loop from latency metrics. Also we moved some of the smaller models to int8 quantized variants which helped throughput.
[01:40] Liam: Nice. Which quantization toolchain did you use? Any experience with QAT vs PTQ?
[01:45] Tereza: Primarily post-training quantization with ONNX Runtime and some INT8 calibration. We experimented with QAT for one of the transformers, but the engineering cost was high relative to the small accuracy gains.
[02:00] Liam: Gotcha. Do you have exposure to lower-level performance work, like CUDA kernels or custom ops?
[02:06] Tereza: Some — I wrote a few custom CUDA kernels when optimizing our feature extraction pipeline — mostly memory-bound ops. Not an expert in kernel fusion but have paired with a performance engineer to prototype a fused attention op.
[02:22] [00:02] Sara (interrupting briefly): sorry small time check, still good on time?
[02:26] Liam: Yep, we're good.
[02:27] Devon: Can you talk about orchestration — what did you use for autoscaling and capacity?
[02:33] Tereza: We used K8s with a custom HPA that considered GPU utilization and queue length; for the Triton fleet we used node pools with varying GPU sizes (A100s for heavy batches, T4s for latency-sensitive small requests). We also had a dedicated VPC and used private subnets for production.
[02:53] Liam: Any experience with private deployments or air-gapped environments?
[02:56] Tereza: Yes, for a regulated client we packaged everything into an offline bundle — container images + infra scripts, and we had to integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management. It was mostly a lift-and-shift, but we added hooks for audit logging.
[03:12] Liam: Great. How do you think about model variants and fallbacks when capacity is constrained?
[03:17] Tereza: We had a policy that fell back to a small distilled model when the primary was unavailable, and we offered degraded responses with a flag indicating lower confidence. We also prioritized premium customers on the routing layer.
[03:28] Devon: Can you describe a recent incident you were oncall for and how you debugged it?
[03:33] Tereza: Sure — we had an outage due to a bad Triton config causing OOMs. It manifested as OOM kills on the GPU nodes and cascading request retries. I pulled metrics (GPU mem, dmon logs), rolled a canary config with reduced batch size, and added additional liveness checks to avoid retries piling up. We then fixed the config in CI and added a regression test.
[03:56] Liam: Nice — what monitoring stack did you use?
[04:00] Tereza: Prometheus + Grafana for infra-level metrics, application spans in Jaeger, and logs in Elastic; we had a lightweight SLO dashboard showing latency buckets.
[04:10] Liam: Good. For the role you'll probably touch compilation/kernel selection and batching heuristics — how comfortable are you designing heuristics to choose kernels or batch sizes based on sequence length distributions?
[04:22] Tereza: Comfortable — we built heuristics driven by a histogram of sequence lengths; for short sequences we used a different kernel path and smaller batch sizes to keep latency low, for long sequences we increased batching and swapped to a memory-optimized kernel. It was empirical: A/B test, measure latency and token cost.
[04:42] Devon: Have you worked on KV cache management for chat-style models?
[04:46] Tereza: Yes, we implemented an LRU-based per-session cache and TTL eviction. One challenge was multi-tenant memory isolation — we put per-tenant quotas to avoid eviction cascades.
[04:58] Liam: Any infra automation: infra-as-code tools? CI/CD for models?
[05:03] Tereza: We used Terraform for infra, Helm for K8s charts, and a models CI that ran unit tests, perf benchmarks and a smoke inference test. Deploys to prod required manual approval for model changes.
[05:17] Liam: How do you validate model quality after a quantization or rollout?
[05:21] Tereza: We have a test harness with holdout prompts and metric thresholds (accuracy, response-time). After a quantized build we run the harness and compare metrics; if any metric regressed beyond threshold we block the rollout. We also capture calibration artifacts and sample diffs.
[05:36] Devon: Scenario: you're asked to support a legacy private customer who needs on-prem inference with strict network isolation, and they want the ability to roll back quickly — what would you propose?
[05:47] Tereza: I'd propose an offline install with orchestration via an air-gapped operator, tenant scoped resources, and a blue-green style deploy using versioned images and a traffic-switching mechanism. For rollbacks, keep last-known-good image and have automated smoke tests to verify post-swap.
[06:05] Liam: Nice. Quick culture fit — how do you prefer to work with product and research partners?
[06:10] Tereza: I like short feedback loops, prototypes that validate hypotheses quickly, and then scale. I collaborate closely with research on evals and with product on acceptance criteria.
[06:21] Devon: What's your preferred interview or team environment? Fast iterations or more planned changes?
[06:25] Tereza: I like pragmatic tradeoffs — ship an experiment, measure, iterate. But heavy infra changes should be more planned.
[06:33] Liam: A few lightning bullets: what's your strongest language/stack?
[06:36] Tereza: Python for orchestration, some Go for infra agents, comfortable with bash, Helm, Terraform and a bit of CUDA C++ for perf work.
[06:45] Liam: Open-source contributions?
[06:47] Tereza: I have two small repos: a batching simulator for inference and a k8s operator that manages GPU nodes; links in my resume.
[06:56] [07:00] Sara: quick recruiter question — are you considering other offers and what's the timeline?
[07:05] Tereza: I'm talking to two companies; hoping to make a decision by end of November.
[07:10] Sara: Great — comp band wise we discussed upfront but we'll share specifics; any visa or relocation constraints?
[07:15] Tereza: No visa constraints, I'm on a US-based team.
[07:18] Liam: Technical follow-up: have you ever written schedulers for batch packing?
[07:23] Tereza: Yes, I implemented a best-fit heuristic that packs different sequence lengths to reduce padding waste; it improved tokens/sec by about 18% in our benchmarks.
[07:36] Devon: What about model sharding and tensor parallelism experience?
[07:40] Tereza: Limited; I helped run a Megatron-LM cluster once, mostly ops side — shard placements and checkpointing were the harder parts.
[07:50] Liam: Do you have any experience with model compilation toolchains (Torch-TensorRT, XLA, TVM)?
[07:57] Tereza: Familiarity with Torch-TensorRT and ONNX optimizations. We tried TVM for some kernels but didn't productionize it.
[08:06] Liam: How do you approach safety and hallucination monitoring in a production system?
[08:11] Tereza: We have a post-processing classifier to detect unsafe outputs and a feedback loop to route flagged outputs to a human review queue. For hallucination, we surfaced provenance and confidence scores and used reranker steps to reduce incorrect answers.
[08:30] Devon: Any experience with billing/costing models per token or per-request?
[08:34] Tereza: Worked on cost dashboards and token accounting. We exposed per-customer cost metrics and used them to gate features for low-margin customers.
[08:44] Liam: Last technical: have you used any Redwood-like product or benchmarks?
[08:49] Tereza: I read some Redwood docs a while back — the prefix caching and routing pieces were interesting. I haven't used the hosted API directly.
[08:58] Liam: Cool. Behaviorals: tell us about a time you disagreed with an engineer and how it resolved.
[09:04] Tereza: we had disagreement on aggressive caching vs fresh results. I built an A/B test which showed slightly stale cache was acceptable for 60% of flows; we landed on a hybrid approach with staleness TTL per route.
[09:20] [09:30] Sara: quick time check — about 10 mins left, we'll do role-specific logistics and wrap.
[09:33] Liam: Two quick scenario questions: 1) A model upgrade causes a 5% drop in a critical metric post-rollout, but logs show no infra changes. Steps? 2) A customer reports 2s p95 on a path that used to be 400ms.
[09:47] Tereza: For 1) roll back, run the model against the pre-upgrade eval set to confirm regression, examine drift in input distribution, check for dependency changes (tokenizer, preprocessing), and compare outputs on a sample. For 2) check routing and queue length, look at recent autoscaler events, verify node health and GPU mem, and trace to see where latency increased — maybe distant storage or network.
[10:20] Devon: Good answers. Any questions for us about the role or team?
[10:24] Tereza: Yes: how much of the role is greenfield vs maintaining existing infra?
[10:28] Devon: It's a mix — there's a new runtime initiative but also a need to stabilize current fleets. You'll own both.
[10:33] Tereza: What's the oncall expectation?
[10:36] Devon: Roughly 1:6 rotation, pager during regional business hours and one weekend every couple months.
[10:44] Tereza: That's reasonable.
[10:46] Liam: Ok final: would you like to ask about career growth or org structure?
[10:50] Tereza: How does success look in the first 6 months?
[10:53] Devon: Deliver a performance or reliability improvement, ship a service or significant automation, and onboard the team to the runbook.
[11:00] Liam: Awesome. We'll wrap — quick recap of next steps: Liam sends a coding exercise and infra diagram, Sara shares comp bands and scheduling. Thanks for your time.
[11:12] Tereza: Thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[11:15] Sara: we'll follow up by end of week.
[11:18] Liam: Bye.
[11:20] Tereza: Bye.
